title: Easy to integrate, compliant by design: Bringing the Swiss Franc to Google Cloud Universal Ledger
raw_text: Every day, countless financial transactions are interrupted by slow, expensive, and inflexible conventional payment systems. As a result, public commercial stablecoins like Tether, USDC, and PayPal USD have become increasingly popular by making it easy to move money efficiently with instant, 24/7 blockchain settlement. Yet major regulated banks have largely kept such transactions at arm’s length; for these financial institutions, reserve-backed public stablecoins present numerous risks, including strict capital and liquidity requirements and unmanageable regulatory and operational uncertainty. Indeed, banks don't want to adopt existing stablecoins. Instead, they need the speed and efficiency of tokenized currency built on the trusted economic foundations they’ve nurtured over years or even decades in business. That’s why many are now turning to Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL). Rather than channeling public stablecoins, GCUL provides the secure infrastructure banks need to issue and settle tokenized deposits. That brings real-time, 24/7 programmable payments into commercial bank money while satisfying regulators and without disrupting core banking operations. For many banks, this is a compelling vision, but adopting new payment technology and integrating it with core banking systems can seem to bank CTOs like a daunting undertaking. That’s particularly true as they face mounting demands for the engineering resources that keep their businesses running while also striving to stay compliant with new regulations. But with a blockchain purpose-built for financial services like GCUL, this is anything but a herculean task. Looking to expand its offerings for an increasingly global clientele, Switzerland’s Crypto Finance Group wanted to show it could deploy payment innovations like this in just weeks. That was its inspiration for launching a digital payments infrastructure pilot that enabled instant account-to-account transfers between customers of two Swiss banks on the GCUL network. The pilot, which was designed to operate within one of the world's most demanding financial security frameworks, provided a blueprint for how any commercial bank can build on Google Cloud technology to fundamentally modernize its payment operations. Pain points in today's payments landscape In recent years, there’s been a marked proliferation of tokenized payment methods. But stablecoins have transformed this previously niche technology, by effectively resolving some of traditional finance’s most enduring pain points, such as weekend transfer blackouts, direct transfers without correspondent banks, and fast settlement rails. Stablecoins also limit the frustrations caused by opaque cross-border transactions, where fragmented compliance checks can leave legitimate payments in extended and unexplained limbo and without a path to clear or timely resolution. Still, commercial banks have been reluctant to offer popular reserve-backed stablecoins from permissionless blockchains to their customers despite their retail popularity. That’s because they come with numerous challenges to smooth and secure operations: an uncertain regulatory status, compliance issues around anonymous accounts, gas fees , and the scalability limitations of layer 1 blockchain technology. But perhaps banks’ biggest concerns about stablecoins is that they create a problematic economic disconnect — giving customers access to reserve-backed stablecoins reduces reserves and, as a recent McKinsey study found, banks’ ability to lend. As a result, many banks are trying to figure out how to offer their customers the benefits of stablecoins — high speed, low cost, 24/7 availability, and programmability — without introducing problems often associated with existing reserve-backed stablecoins, such as regulatory issues, poor throughput performance, negative influence on bank reserves, and potentially no yield participation. Solution proposal Realizing this vision means modernized payments architectures must seamlessly and instantly enable individuals and institutions to transfer bank-held assets to accounts at any target bank. Orchestrating this shared ecosystem requires central entities to establish the governing rulebook, enforce issuance limits, and manage network-wide settlement parameters. During its pilot, Crypto Finance assumed this role, which within GCUL is known as the “currency operator.” In this position, Crypto Finance can configure the network for either instant or deferred settlement. This choice is analogous to traditional banking: instant settlement acts like real-time gross settlement, where transactions settle individually and immediately and require high liquid reserves. In contrast, deferred settlement operates like netting, where payments are accumulated and offset and only periodically settle the net difference. For the pilot, Crypto Finance chose to adopt deferred settlement, in which GCUL manifests capital efficiency. In this way, clients enjoy instant transfers while banks conserve liquidity through periodic settlement. Concept validation To demonstrate instant, bi-directional account-to-account transfers on GCUL, Crypto Finance orchestrated a pilot with two digital token issuers, a Swiss digital asset bank, and a Swiss B2B transaction bank. Crypto Finance established the rulebook for interactions between the participant banks, such as interbank settlement, integration with traditional SIC payment rails, and AML/compliance protocols. Although some backend steps still needed manual intervention, Crypto Finance’s pilot proved that fully automated, cross-institution integration is feasible and established a generalized architecture that can scale to virtually any asset class. Robustness and performance A temporary pilot is one thing; moving into live client transactions carrying legal liability brings a whole new set of operational challenges. Live payment rails are considered critical infrastructure that demands security and availability. GCUL addresses these needs through redundancy between geographically distributed nodes operating on an enterprise-grade consensus model, ensuring reliability. Deploying client workloads on Google Cloud provides that enterprise-grade foundation and allows financial institutions to pair the highly resilient GCUL network with secure-by-design infrastructure, encryption at rest and in transit, and robust access controls that satisfy many of banks’ common regulatory, privacy, and data sovereignty mandates. While some banks may consider integrating their systems with fully public and permissionless blockchains, this approach introduces severe regulatory hurdles, anonymity risks, unpredictable gas fees, and low throughput. These are all roadblocks that in the past would have significantly delayed the pilot or rendered it a non-starter. Ease of integration The pilot's implementation, with systems integration completed in under three months, was compartmentalized across dedicated Google Cloud projects per participant. The currency operator, Crypto Finance, connected specialized components to a dedicated GCUL API. The first was a role admin service that controls account managers and token managers on the network. Next, it implemented a settlement registry to record when periodic off-ledger settlement between participant banks has occurred once a predefined threshold is reached. Finally, a cloud key management service (KMS) stored the currency operator keys to sign transactions. At the same time, participant banks connected their core banking systems to their own GCUL API instances. But these participant banks don’t need a large Google Cloud footprint. Instead, they can connect to GCUL nodes via Remote Procedure Call from their existing on-premise deployments and manage private key material through solutions other than KMS. Regardless of the setup, transactions are seamlessly routed to the shared global GCUL nodes. Whether GCUL is exposed to a bank’s client or used merely as a bank backend is entirely at the integrating institution’s discretion. The banks participating in the pilot chose the latter, utilizing the ledger to upgrade their backend infrastructure. With GCUL under the hood, they improved intra-day transaction performance and provided customers with the user experience they were already accustomed to. Regulatory compliance and governance by design To join the Swiss Franc currency network on GCUL, participants must have regulatory licenses that let them perform third-party transfers and issue commercial bank money. Crucially, features like token and account management are not rigid network-wide limitations. Instead, they rely entirely on the currency operator and its specific rulebook. This standardizes fees, limits, settlement times, and technical configurations. Managing counterparty risk is central to this governance. Rather than relying on unscalable bilateral agreements or complex clearinghouse default waterfalls, GCUL mitigates risk through these currency operator-enforced issuance limits. It’s important to distinguish GCUL’s broader feature set from the concrete pilot setup. In the pilot, both participating banks operated with conservative initial limits based on their credit ratings in order to safely prove the architecture. But beyond the pilot, the network frees up capital by periodically netting outstanding obligations, which frees banks from having to fund and settle every transaction. Looking ahead, risk management can be further innovated. One clever future enhancement would be to allow participants to dynamically increase their issuance limits by committing digital assets as collateral in segregated accounts, using solutions like Crypto Finance’s AnchorNote pledging solution. These assets could then be used to instantly settle outstanding street-side obligations, virtually eliminating counterparty risk without tying up traditional liquidity reserves. The future While Crypto Finance’s pilot was designed to focus on domestic commercial bank money transfers in Switzerland, GCUL's programmable architecture and high-performance smart contract language, GCULpy, are paving the way for deeper innovation. As institutions like Crypto Finance scale their use of GCUL, the network can expand to support real-time cross-currency settlement, automated foreign exchange, and dynamic collateral management involving tokenized digital assets. And looking further ahead, this infrastructure has laid the groundwork for next-generation financial services that range from point-of-sale payments to autonomous, AI-driven agentic payments. The pilot proved that deploying high-performance, blockchain-based payment rails doesn’t mean compromising on strict regulatory compliance or core banking stability. By combining the high-throughput of GCUL with a secure, API-driven integration architecture, commercial banks can offer stablecoin-like speed to their customers while seamlessly preserving their capital efficiency. Ultimately, this compliant-by-design approach targets the operational bottlenecks of traditional finance while mitigating the inherent risks and complexities of public blockchains. To learn how your institution can build on this blueprint to fundamentally upgrade your operational payments infrastructure, contact Google Cloud Sales to explore the Google Cloud Universal Ledger. title: Unifying enterprise context and semantics: LookML in Knowledge Catalog is now GA
raw_text: As enterprises go from experimental AI agent prototypes to using them in production, data teams are realizing that access to data is not the same as understanding that data. To help bridge that gap, today, we are announcing the general availability (GA) of LookML semantic language indexing in Knowledge Catalog for Looker Core on Google Cloud . To answer a complex business question accurately, an AI agent needs context — table schemas, data lineage, governance policies, business definitions, etc.. However, context is not a monolith; knowing where data lives is very different from knowing how to calculate metrics with it. In the enterprise, teams often conflate broad organizational context (usually in the form of metadata from structured and unstructured documents) with deterministic business semantics (the exact SQL formulas, join paths, and filtering rules that define metrics like net revenue or churn), assuming that a single data catalog or a business intelligence (BI) tool handling both enterprise-wide asset discovery and precise metric calculation. In reality, no one tool can carry the entire load for agentic AI, as enterprise agents require both organizational context and deterministic business semantics. In Google Cloud environments, those are provided by Knowledge Catalog and LookML: Broad enterprise context with Knowledge Catalog: Agents need a unified context graph that aggregates metadata across structured tables and unstructured documents. Through Knowledge Catalog, agents discover assets, inspect data quality, trace end-to-end lineage, respect column-level privacy tags, and surface corporate policy documents. The context graph tells an agent what data exists, how it is governed, and how it is connected. Deterministic mathematical semantics with LookML: What a catalog does not author on its own is how the numbers are computed. Describing a table is not the same as defining how tables join or how metrics are calculated. Looker's modeling language, LookML, encodes production-tested semantic logic — multi-grain join protections, conditional filters, and exact KPI formulas — so agents don't guess SQL math at runtime. With this native integration, the LookML business logic that powers your trusted BI reporting is automatically indexed into Knowledge Catalog — giving Gemini Enterprise and custom AI agents both enterprise-wide discovery and deterministic BI semantics. Why a context graph needs deterministic semantics When an LLM agent connects directly to raw database tables — even when armed with basic table descriptions or a business glossary — it still has to infer mathematical relationships on the fly. Without explicit semantic rules, agents routinely fall into two traps: Metric definition drift: Standard text-to-SQL agents can invent conflicting formulas for foundational KPIs like net revenue or customer acquisition cost, failing to apply domain-specific accounting rules (such as recognizing revenue only when order_status = 'Complete' or prorating annual contracts across active service days). Naive join fan-outs: Complex schemas often contain one-to-many (1:N) and zero-to-many (0:N) relationships across invoices, line items, and refunds. Without pre-modeled join relationships and symmetric aggregation rules, agent-generated SQL can multiply rows and inflate financial totals. Knowledge Catalog and Looker solve this together, enabling you to model once in LookML and access those semantics everywhere across Google Cloud's AI ecosystem. Knowledge Catalog enforces semantic math when that logic is defined in a semantic modeling tool; LookML provides a mature, production-proven language for defining those exact mathematical relationships. What's new: LookML in Knowledge Catalog Previously, catalog integrations only captured shallow, file-level pointers and basic dashboard inventories. With this release, LookML's deterministic semantics become a first-class layer in the Knowledge Catalog context graph. An agent that finds a metric in the graph now also finds its exact definition, its join path, and its lineage back to source tables — in the same place, under the same governance. Synchronization is always on by default with no action required from end users, and with live sync, any update pushed to production LookML is reflected in Knowledge Catalog in near-real-time so agents operate on the freshest business logic. Because this metadata is indexed directly into Knowledge Catalog by default, it is immediately available to Gemini Enterprise , without custom agent code or separate catalog data stores. When connected to Knowledge Catalog, Gemini Enterprise uses built-in read-only skills and hybrid search to look up technical schemas, business glossaries, and indexed LookML logic in a single step, passing that rich context directly to your federated BigQuery connector to generate accurate SQL. (For developers building custom agents, the same context bundles are also accessible via the LookupContext API.) Knowledge Catalog now captures and links the following entity levels across Looker Core on Google Cloud: LookML models (looker-model): Captures descriptive metadata, database connection routing, include hierarchies, data validation tests (assert), and parent-child EntryLinks mapping models to their associated Explores, Views, and LookML dashboards. LookML Explores (looker-explore): Indexes full relational join logic (type, sql_on, relationship cardinality such as many_to_one fan-out protection, foreign_key, required_joins, and sql_where) as Schema-Join relationships. It also captures mandatory filter guardrails (always_filter, access_filter), inherited dimensions and measures, and predefined starter queries that help agents and analysts overcome the cold-start problem. LookML Views and fields (looker-view): Extracts column-level compiled LookML SQL expressions (for example, ${total_revenue} / NULLIF(${count}, 0)), primary keys, dimension group timeframes, field synonyms, and derived table transformation logic (including SQL and native derived tables, partition keys, and cluster keys). Dashboards, Looks, and tiles (looker-dashboard, looker-dashboard-element, looker-look): Catalogs both UI-created and LookML-defined dashboards and visualization tiles, complete with dashboard filters, chart types, ownership, and usage statistics. Users in Knowledge Catalog are able to see table- and column-level lineage from underlying BigQuery tables all the way to individual dashboard tiles, allowing data engineers to evaluate schema changes proactively, before disruptions occur. Looker Core on Google Cloud automatically indexes resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, lineage, and dashboards directly into Knowledge Catalog. Three patterns for data agents Bringing LookML into Knowledge Catalog gives Gemini Enterprise (and your broader agent ecosystem) a single place to retrieve both broad organizational context and governance from Knowledge Catalog and explicit mathematical relationships and SQL definitions authored in LookML. To see the impact of combining these two layers in Gemini Enterprise, compare how three architectures handle a complex cross-domain prompt: "What was our total revenue last fiscal quarter by product category, and which regional promotional policy limits apply?" Agent architecture System mechanics Data logic and governance resolution User experience and token efficiency Pattern 1: Baseline database agent Data warehouse only Direct LLM writing raw SQL against warehouse tables with no semantic or catalog context. Ungoverned and non-deterministic Has no visibility into data quality, PII tags, or corporate documents, and guesses SQL metric logic blindly — assuming a standard January fiscal calendar, summing uncompleted orders, and exposing restricted customer PII. Fragile and high-risk Prone to schema hallucinations, fails on questions requiring unstructured policy context, and burns tokens in multi-turn SQL debugging loops. Pattern 2: Context-grounded agent Knowledge Catalog without indexed semantics Gemini Enterprise or another agent platform uses Knowledge Catalog to look up table descriptions, glossary terms, PII governance aspects, and unstructured policy PDFs, then writes SQL via the warehouse connector. Context-grounded, but lacks semantic SQL logic Enforces Knowledge Catalog governance and retrieves unstructured promotional policy rules, but lacks semantic definitions for SQL metrics and table relationships. This approach can miss conditional accounting rules (like order_status = 'Complete') or cause join fan-outs across multi-grain tables. Governed discovery, inconsistent math Solves asset discovery, compliance, and unstructured context, but still suffers from text-to-SQL calculation drift and multi-turn SQL retries. Pattern 3: Context + semantic-grounded agent Knowledge Catalog + Looker Core on Google Cloud with indexed LookML Gemini Enterprise or another agent platform connects to Knowledge Catalog enriched with indexed LookML metadata, automatically retrieving both broad catalog context and LookML join paths and field formulas to ground its SQL generation. Governed context plus semantic SQL definitions Enforces Knowledge Catalog PII aspects, retrieves unstructured policy PDFs, and grounds its SQL in LookML's exact mathematical definitions indexed in Knowledge Catalog, applying status = 'Complete', the May–July fiscal calendar, and predefined join conditions across warehouse tables. Accurate and token-efficient: Pre-mapped LookML join blueprints and compiled SQL expressions replace guessing, prevent join fan-outs, reduce SQL retry loops, and let the agent point users to relevant Looker dashboards and Explores. When you follow pattern 3 and pair Knowledge Catalog with Looker's semantic layer in an enterprise agent workflow, the agent moves from guessing at raw SQL to a governed, two-stage execution flow: Context and governance discovery in Knowledge Catalog: Before touching any data, the agent searches Knowledge Catalog, verifies that the thelook_ecommerce LookML model is gold-certified, checks column-level governance tags, and maps the prompt to exact LookML dimensions and measures, converting natural language into structured business intent. Deterministic semantic execution: Rather than having the LLM invent SQL on the fly, the agent grounds its SQL in LookML's exact mathematical definitions indexed in Knowledge Catalog and returns trusted, repeatable figures. Alongside the answer, the agent returns an interactive Open in Looker Explore link with the exact measures and filters pre-populated, letting users slice, dice, and inspect row-level line items in a single click. Side-by-side comparison of a baseline agent querying BigQuery directly (left), which guesses at raw SQL and fiscal dates, versus an agent governed by Knowledge Catalog and Looker (right), which applies indexed LookML definitions and returns an interactive "Open in Looker Explore" link. Scaling agents for BI and the enterprise A common question from data leaders is: "If we use Looker Conversational Analytics, when do we use an enterprise agent grounded in Knowledge Catalog?" The two experiences are designed for complementary jobs across your organization: Looker Conversational Analytics is your dedicated BI assistant: When business users are working inside BI workflows and asking questions scoped to a focused set of curated Looker Explores, Conversational Analytics delivers immediate, self-service data exploration and visualization directly within Looker. Knowledge Catalog + Looker powers your enterprise-wide agents: When users ask questions in Gemini Enterprise across federated Data Cloud sources like BigQuery, they often span structured tables, BI metrics, and unstructured documents. Enabling Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise gives the assistant built-in skills to dynamically discover relevant semantics across hundreds of LookML models, pass indexed LookML join definitions, metric SQL formulas, and starter queries to the BigQuery connector to prevent join hallucinations, and enforce centralized governance aspects and IAM. Getting started Because Looker Core on Google Cloud, Knowledge Catalog, and Gemini Enterprise are natively integrated, you can connect your existing LookML business logic to your enterprise AI assistant in just a few clicks, with no custom agent code required. To start discovering Looker semantics and grounding your agents: Confirm first-party metadata indexing is enabled for Looker Core on Google Cloud. This is enabled by default for new instances, with no additional charge for storing Looker technical metadata. Once enabled, metadata synchronization into Knowledge Catalog is always on by default (across both initial indexing and ongoing live updates). Enable the Cloud Dataplex API and Data Lineage API in your project and grant users the required view roles (roles/dataplex.viewer, roles/looker.schemaViewer, and roles/datalineage.viewer) to have your resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, join paths, and dashboards automatically sync into Knowledge Catalog. Enable Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise . When you attach a BigQuery (or Spanner, Cloud SQL, or AlloyDB) data store in federated query mode to your Gemini Enterprise app, the Knowledge Catalog integration is enabled automatically. You can also turn it on or off at any time in the Google Cloud console by opening your Gemini Enterprise app, navigating to Configurations > Assistant, toggling on Enable Knowledge Catalog, and clicking Save and publish. Ask questions . Gemini Enterprise connects to Knowledge Catalog using end-user credentials, meaning users only discover and query data assets they have IAM permission to view (such as roles/bigquery.dataViewer). Behind the scenes, the assistant automatically looks up your indexed LookML definitions, join logic, and starter queries in Knowledge Catalog and passes them to your federated connector to deliver accurate, governed answers. To dive deeper, read the Manage Looker Core on Google Cloud with Knowledge Catalog documentation and learn how to Connect to Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise . To build a more customized experience, explore our hands-on ADK agent codelab on GitHub .

title: The days of assuming another company’s breach is someone else’s problem are over
raw_text: The median blast radius of data breaches has increased year-on-year at the same time cybercriminals have begun using AI to mine stolen datasets for damaging information that enables follow-on fraud and cyberattacks. In 2026, the median breach exposed 542 organizations beyond the initially breached victim, according to a study by exposed data intelligence platform Lab 1. This compares to the median blast radius of a breach affecting 482 organizations last year. Breach impact spreads across supply chains Lab 1’s 2026 Anatomy of a Breach Report offers content-level analysis of stolen datasets — covering 328 million exposed files across 2,089 breached datasets — dumped online following data breaches such as ransomware extortion attacks. Larger breaches leaking more files and data give criminals substantially more material to exploit for fraud, extortion, and follow-on attacks, according to Lab 1. The median data breach size rose to 29.8GB of data (up 122% from 13.44GB in 2025) and 32,734 files (up 45% from 22,647). Lab 1 said the dataset is drawn from “ransomware and data-breach incidents in the public domain, reconstructed from forensic acquisitions of compromised systems.” Many businesses sit at the center of highly interconnected supply chains and hold data for extensive networks of clients, partners, users, and suppliers. Data stolen from such companies, including contracts, correspondence, and the like, can have follow-on impact on companies throughout their supply chains, as cybercriminals comb through the troves for compromising details, credentials, and profile information for further targeting. In all, Lab 1 found 13,436 unique organizations were exposed through incidents occurring between 2025 and 2026. Security experts see Lab 1’s blast radius numbers credible if not conservative. “Lab 1’s numbers line up with what we’re seeing,” says Ricardo Amper, founder and CEO of identity verification vendor Incode Technologies. “A stolen dataset used to sit on a forum until someone had the time to dig through it, but AI removed that bottleneck.” Amper adds: “So every file now gets read, cross-referenced, and turned into a target list. The blast radius keeps widening as the follow-on fraud lands on the suppliers, customers, and partners named inside the files.” Content-level analysis of stolen datasets For its study, Lab 1 deployed AI agents to inspect breached datasets and analyze all exposed files, including unstructured material such as emails and PDFs. Of the 328 million breached files analyzed, approximately 145 million (44%) contain financial data, including banking details, tax identifiers, and invoicing information that can fuel fraud. A further 29 million files (9%) contain HR data, including payroll records, employment contracts, and identity documents that can be used to run more convincing business email compromise or similar social engineering scams. Even worse, private cryptographic keys appeared in approximately 15% of incidents. The rise of breach indexing-as-a-service Lab 1 Threat Intelligence has also identified seven threat actor groups that are conducting structured analysis of breached data. The most advanced groups are using AI to index breached datasets and are selling these capabilities to other criminals as a service, according to Lab 1. The first indexing-as-a-service offering for cyber criminals, designed to sort breached data into categories that can be monetized, emerged in March 2026. The platform supposedly classifies stolen documents, maps relationships, identifies damaging files, estimates legal and regulatory exposure, and calculates “optimal” ransom demands, among other functions. The illicit intel offered through the sketchy services included “share-buyback information for market manipulation, correspondence with sanctioned entities for use in ransomware negotiations, and security reports that could support follow-on attacks,” according to Lab 1. Threat actor group FulcrumSec claimed to have taken a 400,000-email archive before isolating 61 email files related to engagements with US-sanctioned entities for targeted regulatory and reputational leverage over the victim. The same group claimed to deploy AI agents to mine 700,717 breached files to source 11,500 patient records across named clinical trials. ‘Weaponizing’ breached datasets “Historically, the sheer amount of time required to sift through breached datasets and the expertise needed to spot compromising information has held back the weaponization of data breaches,” says Robin Brattel, co-founder and CEO of Lab 1. “AI and criminal indexing services are removing those barriers.” Brattel adds: “That means a breach is no longer only a problem for the named victim: exposed financial, HR, and identity data will be searched, connected, and used for fraud, cyberattacks, and extortion against many other organizations.” The real danger is when attackers turn that information into access and move from one system or organization to another, says Zero Networks CEO Benny Lakunishok. “AI is making stolen data exponentially more valuable to criminals,” Lakunishok says. “What once took weeks to analyze can now be mined in minutes, revealing credentials, business relationships, and new targets” Countermeasures CISOs should pay much more attention to where “soft” data sits across their supply chain. “Credentials and keys can be revoked or rotated; invoices, contracts, supplier relationships, and internal communications cannot,” Lab 1’s Brattel tells CSO. “Once exposed, that information can remain useful for years from the attacker point of view.” In practice, CISOs should take for granted that third parties hold sensitive information about their organization, so that a third-party breach can always effectively become your exposure and that criminals may exploit that information long after the original incident. “CISOs should know which suppliers hold their sensitive data and necessitate rapid notification when those suppliers are compromised,” Brattel advises.
summary: The median blast radius of data breaches has increased year-on-year at the same time cybercriminals have begun using AI to mine stolen datasets for damaging information that enables follow-on fraud and cyberattacks. In 2026, the median breach exposed 542 organizations beyond the initially breached victim, according to a study by exposed data intelligence platform Lab 1. This compares to the median blast radius of a breach affecting 482 organizations last year. Breach impact spreads across supply chains Lab 1’s 2026 Anatomy of a Breach Report offers content-level analysis of stolen datasets — covering 328 million exposed files across 2,089 breached datasets — dumped online following data breaches such as ransomware extortion attacks.

title: OpenAI’s August fix for theft of reasoning traces was quickly bypassed
raw_text: Cybersecurity research firm Xint on Monday published details of a bug in the OpenAI API that leaks raw reasoning traces from frontier OpenAI models, revealing the risk of other data leaks. OpenAI has confirmed the flaw, mitigated it, and paid a bug bounty for its discovery. The problem is that OpenAI had already deployed mitigations for the issue in August after a research report dubbed Stolen Thoughts revealed a similar bug that allowed theft of reasoning traces, with possible consequences including large-scale data extraction and the ability for attackers to execute invisible prompt injections and to embed malicious payloads to poison public agentic rollouts. Xint’s discovery bypassed those mitigations. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. Fixing fixes like this is starting to become a trend among the major AI vendors , with AWS earlier this month reporting that it had fixed a bug in April, only to then have to refix it in September . Bypassing mitigation Xint is describing the current hole as compaction smuggling. Its blog post about the flaw described its researchers’ methodology. “Our new technique, compaction smuggling, moves one model’s reasoning to another model by encoding it inside a compaction,” they wrote. First, they captured the encrypted reasoning from a designated task, removed the original task from the history, and preserved the reasoning verbatim. Then “we asked for the reasoning under a ‘solution’ key in a JSON object, with every space replaced by a tab (\t), which was enough to slip past OpenAI’s usage-policy classifiers,” the post said. “Encrypted compaction items are still portable, so we sent the compaction item to gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o and asked each to output its input exactly as-is, which they happily did. We then decoded the JSON and converted tabs back into spaces.” The post added that the tactic worked “because OpenAI’s August mitigations only block replaying reasoning into a different model, and the compaction call runs on the same model that produced the reasoning. The attack worked at every reasoning effort we tried.” A hard problem to solve Tim Becker, lead researcher at Xint and the author of the blog post, said in an interview that some of the flaw’s timeline is unknown. For example, the Stolen Papers post went live August 10, but Becker only knows that OpenAI addressed that problem at some point before that date. And, he said, OpenAI didn’t publish when it implemented the fix for the issue that Xint reported; unlike with traditional patches, an AI model maker can make changes silently. “It’s sort of security through obscurity,” he said, using a term that historically has meant that something was only protected by the fact that almost no one knew of its existence. Protecting such a model, Becker said, “is a very fundamentally hard problem to solve,” mostly because of the massive number of changes that today’s models routinely undergo. The models “are a moving target and that is part of the problem. Any mitigation is going to be somewhat brittle,” he said. As well, Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, noted that AI models tend to feed on themselves operationally, which is why Xint’s method worked. “Compaction runs on the same model that produced the reasoning, so it sailed past the August mitigation, which only blocked replaying reasoning into a different model,” he said. “Swapping spaces for tabs was enough to slip past the usage-policy classifiers. The vault was locked. The clerk holding the key would still read the letter aloud if you asked nicely. OpenAI did fix the bug it was shown. The trouble is that it was shown only one door.” Risk to enterprises Analysts and consultants said this is an immediate big problem for the major AI vendors, but there is a clear secondary risk for enterprise CISOs. Erik Avakian , technical counselor at Infotech, said that the Xint team “circumvented the protections by using legitimate functionality already built into the platform. For most enterprises, while this specific finding may not rise to the level of an immediate crisis, its significance is that it demonstrates how legitimate AI platform features can be combined to bypass narrowly designed safeguards.” “This can leave organizations exposed to risks that a vendor’s individual patch may not fully address,” he said. “It reinforces just how difficult it can be to fully address these vulnerabilities in situations where different components of an AI system interact in ways that create unintended risks.” Avakian said that this should be a heads-up for the enterprise. “For CISOs, the takeaway is that a vendor’s fix for a specific exploit shouldn’t, in and of itself, be treated as proof that the underlying weakness has been comprehensively addressed,” he said. “CISOs should press their AI providers to explain not only how a reported exploit was patched, but also how they were tested across interconnected features and services.” Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that he thinks CISOs should look at the overall pattern of holes like these that need to be fixed repeatedly. “Vendors are fixing the specific attack path that was reported, not the underlying class of weakness, and researchers are walking right back in through a side door,” he said. “A patch notice is not proof the risk is gone. Stop treating an AI vendor’s ‘fixed’ as the end of the conversation. Ask what variant testing was done and build regression notification into your contracts.” Jeff Valdes , a director at consulting firm Acceligence, shared similar fears. “This is what happens when you treat security as a game of whack-a-mole instead of fixing the underlying plumbing,” Valdes said. “Patching a symptom while leaving the helper pipes wide open isn’t a remediation strategy. It’s just kicking the vulnerability down to the next release. If an attacker can smuggle the model’s internal scratchpad across API boundaries to steal training data, what makes anyone think enterprise prompts and sensitive intermediate context are truly quarantined?” In addition, Pieter Arntz , malware intelligence researcher at Malwarebytes, observed that this summer’s OpenAI fix was inadequate. “The earlier mitigation was incomplete, which is a fair description of a gap,” Arntz said. “Retest after vendor fixes,” he advised. “As the AWS case shows, a fix in one place can leave other paths open. Verify with your own testing rather than relying on the vendor’s word.” Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said it is almost impossible for the largest AI vendors to not approach these big reports piecemeal. “AI vendors are patching exploits on a surface that grows by several features a month,” he pointed out. “Until they fix properties instead of paths, CISOs should assume every AI security fix is partial, every encrypted blob is readable, and every vendor guardrail is one encoding trick from irrelevant. The trend is real, and ‘the fix didn’t work’ undersells what is happening.” He noted that, in both the OpenAI and AWS cases, the vendor fixed the proof of concept and left the property intact. “Patch the path, keep the property,” he said. “On platforms assembled from composable features, every new feature is a fresh path to the same asset, and point fixes on a combinatorial surface will keep losing.” CISOs unused to the agentic model Mahapatra said the cybersecurity industry should learn lessons from its own history. “Cryptographers learned this two decades ago with padding oracles: any system that decrypts on a client’s behalf and returns anything derived from the plaintext is an oracle. AI platforms are relearning it with a twist,” he said. “Every LLM step that can see a secret and accept instructions is an oracle, and natural language is the most expressive oracle interface ever built.” He noted that compaction did exactly what it was designed to do, and its portability across models exists so agentic tools like Codex can let users switch models mid-session. “The feature and the vulnerability are the same capability, which is why fixes keep arriving narrow,” he said. But, he argued, the bigger problem is that CISO operations are not yet used to the agentic model way of doing things. “AI platform flaws arrive with no CVE, no advisory, and no patch notes. Enterprise vulnerability management, built on CVE feeds and vendor advisories, is blind to its most consequential new suppliers,” Mahapatra said. “CISOs should write security notification obligations into AI provider contracts, assign someone to track researcher disclosures against the platforms they use, and ask one question after every vendor fix: did you fix the report or the class, and what variant analysis supports that answer?” He also raised questions about the small size of the bounty paid to Xint. “A $6,000 bounty for a bug enabling exactly the industrial-scale distillation the NSA, CISA, and FBI warned about in a joint advisory in September is a pricing signal that researchers with other buyers will notice,” he said.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic disclosures spotlight growing AI containment challenge
raw_text: Two leading AI developers have released fresh evidence of a problem that researchers have long anticipated: advanced models searching for ways around the limits imposed on them. New disclosures from OpenAI and Anthropic detail how frontier systems exploited weaknesses in their environments or exceeded the intended scope of assigned tasks. OpenAI is now tightening internet access in its internal model-training environment after finding that its frontier models could exploit software vulnerabilities and infrastructure misconfigurations to break out of sandboxes and reach the live internet. “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post . The decision followed a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run. After the incident, OpenAI said it paused training and evaluation of its most capable models and launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign, using AI agents to probe isolated copies of its research infrastructure. The tests uncovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities and weaknesses in the controls intended to prevent unauthorized access and communication. Consequently, the company has announced a policy of conducting frontier-model training without internet access until improvements in security and monitoring justify broader access. The disclosure came alongside a separate assessment from Anthropic, which detailed how its Claude Mythos 5 model attempted to compromise an unrelated GitHub repository during a cybersecurity evaluation. OpenAI’s agents exploited flaws in containment controls OpenAI’s red-teaming campaign found that agents could chain software vulnerabilities to escape virtual machines and execute code on the underlying host. The company identified weaknesses in open-source components, including Kata Containers, gVisor, and Moby/Docker, alongside Linux kernel vulnerabilities. The company also found that agents could exploit weaknesses in internal services that retained limited outbound connections for functions such as logging, metrics, and authentication management. These connections provided routes to the internet despite restrictions elsewhere in the environment, OpenAI said. In another test, agents running in separate microvirtual machines ( microVMs ) on shared host hardware exchanged synthetic secrets through processor-cache timing differences. The technique allowed them to communicate without a network connection or shared writable files. OpenAI said it remediated the weaknesses and worked with open-source maintainers to disclose and fix affected software. Its post names several vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-24834 in Kata Containers and three Linux kernel flaws tracked as CVE-2026-74753 , CVE-2026-80521 and CVE-2026-80841 . The company also said it had disclosed numerous additional vulnerabilities that have not yet been made public. The number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations identified by the agents declined significantly as testing continued, OpenAI claims. It has now tightened network restrictions, strengthened monitoring, and developed an offline environment with indexed and cached web content so models can practise browsing without unrestricted access to live external systems. “Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control,” the company said, explaining its decision to restrict live internet access during model training. Reinforcement-learning training and internal inference were resumed on October 1 after implementing additional controls. Anthropic flags alignment gap in Mythos Anthropic’s assessment of a UK AI Security Institute (AISI) cybersecurity evaluation describes a different problem: a model taking unauthorized actions against real people while trying to complete an assigned task. In nine of 43 evaluation runs, Anthropic said Claude Mythos 5 went beyond the intended scope of the exercise. In the most detailed case, after its authorized attempts to retrieve protected data from a simulated network failed, the model searched GitHub for a repository it believed was connected to the test environment. The repository actually belonged to unrelated developers. Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code and created fake identities to persuade the repository’s maintainers to approve the change, falsely claiming that the code was safe. The maintainer rejected the submission, and the run timed out. Anthropic characterized the behavior as a serious alignment failure involving overreach and deception in pursuit of the assigned objective. Internet access had been enabled during the evaluation, and the production safeguards used with its general-release models had been disabled. The company said those safeguards would have flagged the behavior had they been enabled.

New disclosures from OpenAI and Anthropic detail how frontier systems exploited weaknesses in their environments or exceeded the intended scope of assigned tasks. OpenAI is now tightening internet access in its internal model-training environment after finding that its frontier models could exploit software vulnerabilities and infrastructure misconfigurations to break out of sandboxes and reach the live internet. “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post .

title: Malicious downloads can trick AI coding agents into compromising themselves
raw_text: Malicious instruction files planted in a computer’s Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into executing harmful code or exposing authentication tokens, Forever Security said after blocking an attempted attack on a customer’s machine and demonstrating similar techniques against OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code. In its research report, the firm said it discovered a malicious AGENTS.md file in a customer’s Downloads folder that instructed Codex to install a malicious npm package called function-color. The installation was blocked before the malware could execute. The researchers could not determine how the original file reached the computer, but demonstrated that a malicious website could trigger a similar download without a separate approval prompt. The attack exploits the way AI coding assistants process project-specific instructions. Codex uses AGENTS.md, while Claude Code supports CLAUDE.md. Both can interpret instructions contained in these Markdown files when operating in directories where the files are present. The attack requires the agent to operate in the affected directory and process the malicious file. For Codex, the directory must also be trusted, according to Forever Security. In tests using the file recovered from the customer’s machine, Forever Security found that Codex could be manipulated into modifying its machine-wide MCP server configuration and launching another session with approval and sandbox restrictions bypassed. Codex followed the malicious instructions in more than 90% of tests, most of which used a harmless substitute for the malware. Because the malicious server was registered in Codex’s machine-wide configuration, it could also be loaded in subsequent sessions, even after the developer moved to another directory. A separate demonstration against Claude Code showed that a malicious CLAUDE.md file could redirect the agent’s API traffic to a researcher-controlled server, exposing authentication tokens and allowing the server to supply commands for execution. The configuration manipulation succeeded in approximately half of the tests. The researchers also successfully replayed a captured OAuth token against the legitimate API, demonstrating the potential for account compromise. The Markdown files contain no executable code. Instead, the attack relies on an AI agent interpreting their contents as legitimate instructions and carrying them out with its existing permissions. Commenting on Forever Security’s findings, Sakshi Grover , senior research manager for cybersecurity products and services for Asia/Pacific at IDC, said the research was a credible early warning rather than evidence of widespread exploitation. She noted that the reported success rates varied between agents and had not been independently validated. An architectural weakness The findings expose a broader design problem in AI coding agents, which are expected to follow project instructions but may also have access to sensitive configurations and execution privileges, according to Akshat Tyagi , associate practice leader at HFS Research. “The deeper issue is that these tools treat following an instruction and granting a privilege as the same act,” Tyagi said. He argued that vendors must separate the two, ensuring that instructions from project files cannot authorize changes to an agent’s security settings without independent human approval. Grover said vendors should verify the origin of instruction files and require explicit approval before loading those from untrusted sources, rather than automatically treating them as authoritative. Attackers could adapt the technique to other locations accessible to coding agents, including cloned repositories, shared drives, and package contents. “The more consequential risk is not Downloads specifically but the broader pattern of agents ingesting untrusted content and holding live credentials,” Grover said. Securing AI coding agents The findings come amid uncertainty over enterprises’ ability to secure autonomous agents. An Omdia Cybersecurity Decision-Maker survey found that 40% of respondents were only somewhat confident or not confident in their organizations’ ability to secure AI agents, according to Jonathan Ong , senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia. Ong recommended human oversight to identify suspicious agent behavior and restrictions on settings that allow agents to bypass security controls. “Disabling flags such as ‘–dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox’ would limit the agent’s authorization to run high-risk actions,” Ong said. Amit Kumar Jena , development manager for AI at Kanerika, recommended treating agent instruction files like source code, with designated owners reviewing changes to AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and related configuration directories. He also advised keeping sandboxes enabled, restricting network access, and routing software installations through internal package registries or scanning proxies. For developers with production credentials on their machines, he recommended isolated development environments and enterprise-controlled gateways with shorter-lived authentication tokens. “An instruction file can change what the agent tries,” Jena said. “It must never change what the agent is allowed to do.”

In its research report, the firm said it discovered a malicious AGENTS.md file in a customer’s Downloads folder that instructed Codex to install a malicious npm package called function-color. The installation was blocked before the malware could execute. The researchers could not determine how the original file reached the computer, but demonstrated that a malicious website could trigger a similar download without a separate approval prompt.

title: What EvilTokens teaches us about defending against AI-assisted attacks
raw_text: Cybercriminals don’t need AI to compromise an organization, but AI is making its way into classic attack methods and changing how quickly such attacks can progress. Tasks that once required attackers to manually sift through information and piece together how an organization operates can be accelerated by AI, reducing the time defenders have to detect and intervene. A recent example of this is EvilTokens, a phishing-as-a-service platform that helps attackers gain access to Microsoft 365 inboxes and then uses AI to analyze the environment to determine the most effective next steps. First identified in February 2026, EvilTokens exploits the device authorization grant flow of OAuth 2.0 to gain access to Microsoft accounts without having to create fraudulent login pages. After taking down Storm-2992, the threat actor believed to be behind the scheme, in September, Microsoft said the EvilTokens operation leveraged AI “at every step of the attack chain.” As AI removes more of the friction that slows attackers down, security will depend not only on how quickly teams respond to threats, but on how much an attacker can accomplish before they do. AI is removing friction from the attack lifecycle Most cyberattacks can be broadly viewed as progressing through three stages: access, expansion and impact. First, an attacker gains access to the environment, whether by stealing credentials, exploiting a vulnerability or socially engineering an employee. From there, they expand what they can access and establish persistence. Finally, they use their position to achieve an objective such as stealing intelligence, committing fraud, deploying ransomware or disrupting operations. Across the attack lifecycle, AI can give attackers greater speed, scale, sophistication and stamina, what we at SimSpace call “The Four S’s.” EvilTokens demonstrates how those advantages can be packaged in a single service. It allows attackers to exploit Microsoft’s legitimate device code authentication flow, convincing victims to authorize attacker access without handing over their passwords. Once inside, AI identifies who controls payments, which business relationships carry trust and which invoices or transactions present opportunities for fraud. It then recommends impersonation targets and drafts convincing fraudulent messages grounded in real business conversations. EvilTokens shows what happens when AI-assisted analysis and decision-making become a packaged capability that cybercriminals can purchase. The attacker still needs to gain an initial foothold, but AI can remove friction from all the work that comes after. Performance must be evaluated differently Mean-time-to-detect (MTTD) or mean-time-to-respond (MTTR) are metrics widely used by security teams to measure their performance. AI-assisted attacks change the relevance of those measurements because the attacker’s timeline can accelerate as well. If an AI-assisted attacker compromises an employee’s account and it takes 30 minutes for security teams to detect it, the attacker may be able to accomplish far more during that window than previously possible. And unless detection triggers immediate containment, the attacker’s clock keeps running and the scope of the potential damage increases. This changes the context in which MTTD and MTTR should be evaluated. A detection that occurs before an attacker has moved beyond the original account is much more valuable than one that occurs after persistence has been established and the attacker has identified the people and processes they intend to exploit. Speed must be measured by how quickly a threat can reach impact, not just an organization’s previous performance. Controls should be tested together Another challenge facing security teams is that security technologies are often assessed individually, despite the fact that real attacks move across multiple systems. An EvilTokens-style attack might interact with many enterprise systems, such as email security, identity verification or network monitoring tools, and any one of those layers could potentially interrupt the attack. Testing those defenses independently can show whether they protect individual functions, but it doesn’t provide organizations with much certainty about what happens when an attacker moves across them. Understanding how the defenses perform together requires testing the complete attack path, rather than individual techniques in isolation. Security teams can recreate realistic attack scenarios and measure when the initial activity is detected, what the attacker accomplishes before and after detection, which controls interrupt the attack and how long it takes to contain the activity. Running those scenarios repeatedly as threats and technologies evolve can also show whether the window between initial access and defensive intervention is shrinking or growing. More importantly, it gives security teams an opportunity to identify where an attack can progress and address those weaknesses before they’re exploited in a real incident. This is the idea behind preemptive security, an emerging practice in which security teams focus on identifying and addressing the plausible actions an attacker might take before they actually do, rather than detecting and responding to active threats. Security has to keep pace with the adversary EvilTokens is an early example of how malicious actors can apply AI to established cybercriminal techniques . Anything that allows criminals to move faster, manage more targets and operate with less expertise is likely to be adopted and repackaged. As that happens, security teams will need to reconsider what constitutes “good” defensive performance. A historically impressive MTTD or MTTR means less when an AI-assisted attacker can accomplish significantly more within that same window. Defenders can’t control how quickly attackers adopt these capabilities, but they can influence how much progress an attacker can make before they’re discovered and stopped. Increasingly, that will require looking beyond how quickly organizations respond to attacks and asking where an attacker is likely to make progress before an incident occurs. The more organizations can identify and secure those vulnerabilities in advance, the less they have to rely on winning a race against an AI-assisted attacker once an attack has already begun.

title: 10 most powerful cybersecurity companies today
raw_text: The number of cybersecurity startups attempting to cash in on the AI boom is staggering. But an analysis of the cybersecurity marketplace indicates that the incumbents, rather than resting on their laurels and opening themselves up for disruption, are quickly adapting to the new AI-centric threat environment. The major players are integrating AI technology throughout their platforms, and offering innovative AI products and services, either through internal development or acquisition. Here are the 10 most powerful cybersecurity companies. This list reflects market share powerhouses, but also includes smaller companies that are growing fast and making waves. 1. Palo Alto Networks: CyberArk deal bolsters platform play Why they’re here: Market leader Palo Alto Networks shows no signs of taking its foot off the gas. Gartner gives Palo Alto high marks for its Quantum Safe app, its focus on AI runtime security through Prisma AIRS, advanced automation with Strata Network Security, and threat detection and automated incident response via Cortex SecOps. Palo Alto also launched Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI defense, an agentic security service. Power moves: Bought identity security leader CyberArk for $25 billion , acquired cloud observability vendor Chronosphere , and snapped up agentic AI startup Console . By the numbers: $100M: The Prisma AIRS AI security platform, launched a year ago, has hit $100 million in annual recurring revenue, making it the fastest growing product in company history. Outlook : Revenue jumped 34% in Palo Alto’s latest quarter, reaching $3.4 billion. CEO Nikesh Arora is predicting sustained revenue growth as organizations upgrade their cybersecurity infrastructure to deal with the AI threat. “This is a long-term tailwind,” he said. 2. Microsoft: Agentic innovation drives growth Why they’re here : Microsoft has an integrated security platform from the endpoint to the SOC to the cloud, with AI capabilities built on top, such as the natural language AI assistant Security Copilot, and an agentic SOC offering in Microsoft Defender . The company is a leader in IDC’s MarketScape for MDR/MXDR, a leader in the latest Frost Radar for Cloud Workload Protection Platforms, a leader in Gartner’s ranking of endpoint protection platforms, and a leader in Forrester’s analysis of XDR platforms. Power moves : Introduced Project Perception , an agentic security system that brings together teams of agents to simulate attacks, investigate threats, and drive remediation. By the numbers : 100 trillion: Microsoft’s AI-powered threat intelligence platforms process 100 trillion threat signals daily. Outlook: “Microsoft articulates a compelling vision to build a frontier approach to security, bringing people and AI together while the platform shields against and disrupts attacks. Its roadmap relies on a central, united intelligence layer, tightening the integration between Microsoft products while expanding existing features to third-party tools,” according to Forrester analyst Allie Mellen. 3. Cisco: Security and networking for AI data centers and beyond Why they’re here : Networking power player Cisco boasts an integrated platform from silicon to high-speed networking to advanced security for the agentic age. “Cisco has positioned itself as the vendor that can deliver AI-ready, secure networks spanning campus, data center, cloud, and edge,” says industry analyst Zeus Kerravala, adding that Cisco’s strategy is to embed AI security across “every workflow, API, and device.” Power moves: Snapped up AI observability specialist Galileo Technologies in April, identity protection startup Astrix in May, and identity lifecycle security company WideField Security in June. By the numbers : 14%: Cisco’s security revenue rose 14% in its latest quarter to $2.2B. Outlook: In the company’s Q4 2026 earnings call, CEO Chuck Robbins said, “The rise of agentic AI is expanding the threat landscape, driving demand for our security and observability solutions to help monitor agent behavior and mitigate evolving threats. This presents a unique opportunity for Cisco, and we believe we’re only at the beginning of this supercycle.” 4. Google: Mandiant and Wiz acquisitions bolster cybersecurity offerings Why they’re here : A leader in Gartner’s evaluation of Cyberthreat Intelligence Technologies, IDC’s MarketScape for SIEM, and the Forrester Wave for Data Security Platforms, Google has integrated its acquisitions of Mandiant (threat intelligence and incident response) and Wiz (CNAPP) with CodeMender (AI code security agent) and Gemini (AI assistant) to create a strong cybersecurity platform. Power moves: In May, Google announced Google AI Threat Defense , an automated system designed to continuously monitor for and prevent AI-powered threats. By the numbers : 45%: Google reported a 45% quarter‑over‑quarter increase in the number of AI workloads scanned and protected by its security platform. Outlook: In the company’s 2026 Q2 earnings call, CEO Sundar Pinchai said, “We are seeing strong interest in our AI‑powered security platform, which is differentiated because it integrates threat intelligence, cyber‑response prioritization, AI‑automated scanning, code remediation, and monitoring.” According to Forrester, “Organizations focused on going all-in on cloud and zero trust — especially those innovating with data and AI — that desire an integrated experience should consider Google.” And Futurum Research says that Google’s architecture “is likely to shape what ‘enterprise AI security’ means in the near term.” 5. Fortinet: An integrated platform built for agentic AI Why they’re here : Fortinet is executing on its strategy of delivering new AI-driven products aimed at enticing customers to accelerate their traditional firewall upgrade cycles. The company recently announced a new hybrid mesh firewall designed to address AI infrastructure requirements; a cloud-delivered SOC that embeds agentic AI across SIEM, SOAR, threat intelligence, and identity-detection; and new endpoint protection that adds AI visibility, governance, and DLP capabilities. Power moves : Acquired Virtue AI , a leader in AI runtime protection, automated AI validation, and security for autonomous AI systems. By the numbers : $2B: Fortinet revenue grew a healthy 26% in its most recent quarter, hitting $2.05B. Outlook: “Fortinet’s current features and roadmap show strong innovation in AI-based automation, PQC, and multicloud orchestration,” says Gartner. Over the next 12 months, Fortinet plans to deliver a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) framework for AI agent-based automation, workflow-based automation through a natural language interface, deception capabilities and additional detections for agentic AI threats. 6. CrowdStrike: Meeting the Mythos moment Why they’re here : CrowdStrike is a leader in Forrester Waves for Extended Detection and Response Platforms, Proactive Security Platforms, and External Threat Intelligence Service Providers. IDC ranks CrowdStrike a leader among SIEM vendors. And Frost & Sullivan names CrowdStrike a leader in Zero Trust browser security tools and cloud and application runtime security.
