title: Bright Security Introduces STAR Fuzzer, Agentic Fuzzing That Writes Its Own Harnesses and Proves Every Finding
raw_text: Built on an evolutionary engine first released in 2018, STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security finds crashes, memory exhaustion and memory-safety bugs in security-critical code without a running application. In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, and in its first month of availability it produced ten published findings in eight projects, including the Crystal standard library, htop and RIOT OS. Bright Security , the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, today announced the official launch of STAR Fuzzer, an agentic application fuzzer that automatically identifies security-critical functions, generates a fuzzing harness for each one, searches for faults with an evolutionary algorithm, and delivers every confirmed finding with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it. STAR Fuzzer is a self-contained mode of the Bright STAR platform and is available now at brightsec.com/fuzzer . Agentic fuzzing applies AI agents to the parts of fuzzing that have traditionally required a specialist: choosing what to test, writing the harness, and deciding which crashes matter. STAR Fuzzer uses AI for those steps and an evolutionary search engine for the fuzzing itself, so the parts that need judgment are automated and the search stays fast, repeatable and evidence based. Why Fuzzing Needed a New Approach Coverage-guided fuzzers such as AFL++ and libFuzzer are proven and widely used, and programs like Google’s OSS-Fuzz have shown how much they can find. But they depend on people to write and maintain a harness for every target and to triage the crashes that come back. That cost has kept fuzzing concentrated in specialist teams and a subset of critical projects. Other testing approaches don’t fill the gap. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tests what an attacker can reach over HTTP, so it rarely exercises the parsing and processing code behind input validation. LLM-based pentesting is effective at known vulnerability patterns but tends to look where a model expects bugs to be. The result is a class of outage-level and memory-safety defects, often triggered by tiny malformed inputs, that most AppSec programs never test for. How STAR Fuzzer compares with traditional coverage-guided fuzzers (such as AFL++ and libFuzzer) and DAST: What it Tests: Traditional fuzzers test functions exposed through a hand-written harness. DAST tests running applications over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions on untrusted-input paths, chosen automatically. Harness: Traditional fuzzers need harnesses written and maintained by engineers. DAST doesn’t use one. STAR Fuzzer generates a harness per function with AI, then verifies it reaches its target. Search: Traditional fuzzers use coverage-guided mutation. DAST sends request-level attack payloads. STAR Fuzzer uses a structure-aware evolutionary search guided by coverage and multiple fitness signals. Running App Needed: Traditional fuzzers, no. DAST, yes. STAR Fuzzer, no. Triage: Manual for traditional fuzzers and built into the scanner for DAST. STAR Fuzzer triages automatically for reachability and impact. Output: Traditional fuzzers return crash inputs and logs. DAST returns a vulnerability report. STAR Fuzzer delivers the file, function and byte-exact payload in a pull request. Fix Validation: Traditional fuzzers need a manual re-run and DAST needs a rescan. With STAR Fuzzer, teams replay the payload. Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss Ask an LLM to audit a parser and it will find the bug classes it already knows from training. The zero-days that survive for years in mature, widely deployed code are the ones that match no known pattern. STAR Fuzzer uses AI to choose targets and build harnesses, but the search that finds the bugs is not an LLM. It doesn’t read the code or guess where a bug might be. It runs the program millions of times, observes what actually happens, and keeps whatever pushes the target into code it hasn’t reached yet. In Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss , Bright Security CTO Bar Hofesh gives four reasons LLM code review does not replace fuzzing for zero-day discovery: Scale: A single fuzzing campaign runs 1 million to 10 million concrete inputs against the compiled target. At about 2,000 tokens per reasoned test case, matching one million executions with an LLM would take about two billion tokens for one target, and each of those test cases would still be a prediction. Speed and Ground Truth: A persistent harness runs hundreds to a few thousand inputs per second per worker, across several parallel workers, so one million executions take minutes to tens of minutes. One LLM reasoning pass over one hypothesis takes several seconds, so one million would take months. The fuzzer also observes real behavior, such as a sanitizer reporting a heap read one byte out of bounds. An LLM has to predict how compiled code behaves, including struct layouts, integer widths, allocator behavior and build flags that aren’t visible in the source. Coverage: STAR Fuzzer’s libxml2 harness reaches about 13,600 code regions in a 5-million-execution run. Coverage feedback shows which regions each input reached, and inputs that reach new code become starting points for deeper search. Code review has no equivalent signal for how much of a large parser it has actually covered. The Unexpected: LLMs, code reviewers and static analyzers look for the same known patterns, so in mature code most of those bugs are already fixed. The fuzzer has no expectations about where a bug should be. The target’s own behavior decides what is interesting. Reproducibility is the other difference. Many plausible-looking LLM findings don’t reproduce, and maintainers need a reproducer before they can act. A fuzzer finding is a reproducer by construction, and Bright Security replays every one in a fresh container before filing it. How STAR Fuzzer Works STAR Fuzzer’s search engine drives any target through a small harness over IPC, so the code under test can be written in C, C++, Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin, Crystal, Node or any language that can read an input and report back. Structure-aware parsing with no per-target grammar: Every seed is parsed into a typed tree of fields by a format-agnostic parsing layer, and the tree serializes back to the original bytes exactly. No grammar or dictionary file is written per target, and each format added to the parsing layer improves every target that uses it. Mutations that get past the first check: Byte-level mutation mostly produces inputs a parser rejects at its first sanity check. Mutating the fields of a valid structured input keeps most executions past framing and validation, so the testing budget is spent on the deeper logic behind them. Evolution with exact replay: Each organism in the population carries a genome, an ordered list of mutations. Each epoch, organisms mutate, run and are scored. Improvements are kept, unproductive changes are reverted, and organisms breed. Replaying a genome reproduces its payload exactly, so every result can be regenerated from a logged random seed. Results from Open-Source Testing Before release, Bright Security ran STAR Fuzzer for two days in an automated pipeline against multiple open source projects, from libraries and applications to low-level binary parsers. 45% of the projects tested had High or Critical issues, and 37% of the vulnerable projects are part of Google’s OSS-Fuzz program. In its first month of availability, STAR Fuzzer produced ten published findings in eight projects written in C, Go, JVM languages and Crystal. Each was replayed in a fresh container before filing: TwelveMonkeys: In the DDS reader, the mipMapCount header field sizes an uncapped array, so a 38-byte file forces a multi-gigabyte allocation (CWE-789). GHSA-fwp7-38wp-mmxw, fixed in 3.15.0. Fider: Upload validation checks an image’s compressed size, then fully decodes it, so a 436 KB PNG expands to about 562 MB. Any authenticated user can trigger it (CWE-409). STAR Fuzzer found it in about 12 minutes, in a release already benchmarked by multiple AI pentesting vendors. GHSA-7cw3-7xh9-529r, fixed in 0.38.0. Crystal standard library (XML): XML::Node#namespace type confusion. ENTITY_DECL is missing from an allowlist, so a field of libxml2’s xmlEntity struct is read as an xmlNs* (CWE-843). GHSA-c267-9cqj-hv9f, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1. Crystal standard library (YAML): YAML::Any#hash overflows the stack on a self-referencing anchor and alias cycle. An 88-byte input causes an uncatchable SIGSEGV (CWE-674). GHSA-fj8w-2r88-5v7w, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1. libsolv: Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-104621 and CVE-2026-104622. Details are under embargo. htop: An out-of-bounds read in the /proc/PID/stat parser, caused by a missing bounds check on field 22 (CWE-125). Fixed (#2101). universal-ctags: A null-pointer member access in foreachEntriesInScope (CWE-476). Fixed in commit 780bd7a (#4497). scrimage: An uncapped width-times-height pixel count lets a 35-byte GIF trigger allocation attempts of about 2 GB, and over 8 GB in a second variant (CWE-789). Fixed in 4.6.8 (#893). RIOT OS: An off-by-one in _dirlist_cb (link_format.c). The bounds check runs after the write, so a NUL byte lands one past the buffer (CWE-193). Fix submitted in PR #22879. Several of these bugs sit in code that looks correct on review. The Fider upload has a size limit, but it measures compressed size. The TwelveMonkeys field reads as image metadata, not as a length. The Crystal allowlist looks complete. The YAML hash function is correct for trees, and the bug is a cycle in the input. The full methodology and results are published in two parts: Part I on brightsec.com, and Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss by Bar Hofesh. Where STAR Fuzzer Fits Best STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security is designed for teams whose code handles untrusted input below the HTTP layer, including: Applications that process uploaded files, images, documents or archives Parsers, serialization code and raw binary protocols Non-web software such as embedded and IoT firmware, desktop applications and backend services Codebases with a growing share of AI-generated code that needs testing beyond pattern matching Security teams that want to confirm static analysis (SAST) findings by exercising the flagged functions live It supports C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal, and runs inside the customer’s environment with no running application, cloud scanner or authentication required. In persistent mode, harness execution is about 51 times faster than running a new process per input. Executive Perspectives “Fuzzing has always found the bugs that matter most, the ones that take a service down or corrupt memory, but it has been too expensive for most teams to run,” said Bar Hofesh, Co-founder and CTO of Bright Security . “The search was never the bottleneck. The harnesses and the triage were. STAR Fuzzer automates both, so the evolutionary engine we built in 2018 can finally run across a whole codebase.””When Nevada opened the Boulder City Bypass in 2018, it took navigation apps months to start sending drivers down it,” Hofesh added. “LLMs auditing code work the same way. They find the bugs they’ve already seen. The zero-days that have lived for years in mature code are the ones nobody has seen before, and that’s exactly where a fuzzer shines.””Security teams are being asked to keep up with code written faster than ever, much of it by AI,” said Gadi Bashvitz, Co-founder and CEO of Bright Security. “Testing that only looks where bugs are expected won’t keep pace. STAR Fuzzer looks everywhere else, and it hands developers the proof they need to fix what it finds.””AppSec teams keep asking us the same thing: if AI is writing more of our code, what’s testing the parts AI can’t, see?” said Eyal Dror, CMO of Bright Security. “STAR Fuzzer is our answer. In its first month it found ten real bugs in mature open-source projects, and everyone came with the exact input that triggers it. That’s proof a developer can act on the same day, not another alert to argue about.” Availability STAR Fuzzer is available now as a mode of Bright STAR. Learn more and book a demo at brightsec.com/fuzzer . Frequently Asked Questions: What is Agentic Fuzzing? Agentic fuzzing uses AI agents to automate the judgment-heavy steps of fuzzing: selecting which functions to test, writing and verifying harnesses, and triaging results. The fuzzing itself is performed by a search engine that mutates inputs to trigger faults. How is STAR Fuzzer Different from AFL++ or libFuzzer? AFL++ and libFuzzer are fuzzing engines that need engineers to write a harness for each target and to triage crashes by hand. STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security selects targets, generates and verifies harnesses, triages faults for reachability and impact, and delivers findings in a pull request with a reproducing payload. Can LLMs Find Zero-Day Vulnerabilities in Parsers? LLMs are effective at known bug classes, such as an unchecked memcpy length or string-built SQL, but they look where their training says bugs should be. In mature code, the bugs that survive are the ones that match no known pattern, which is where evolutionary, coverage-guided fuzzing is strongest. Why Use a Fuzzer Instead of LLM Code Review? A fuzzing campaign runs millions of real executions against compiled code and observes what happens, while an LLM predicts behavior from the source. Matching one million executions with LLM reasoning would take about two billion tokens per target. Every fuzzer finding also comes with an input that reproduces it. How are STAR Fuzzer Findings Verified? Every finding comes with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it, and Bright Security replays each one in a fresh container before filing it. Any result can also be regenerated from a logged random seed. Does STAR Fuzzer Need Grammars or Dictionary Files? No. A format-agnostic parsing layer turns each seed into a typed tree of fields, so no per-target grammar or dictionary is required. Does STAR Fuzzer Replace DAST? No. DAST tests a running application from the outside in, over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions from the inside out, without a running application. Bright STAR runs both, with the same agent and the same pull-request output. What Kinds of Bugs Does STAR Fuzzer Find? Crashes, hangs, out-of-memory conditions and unbounded allocations, memory-safety bugs such as out-of-bounds reads and off-by-one writes, type confusion, stack overflows from recursive input structures, and algorithmic-complexity blow-ups, including decompression bombs triggered by inputs of a few dozen bytes. Which languages does STAR Fuzzer Support? C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal. Its AI-powered Bright STAR platform integrates security directly into the development lifecycle, automating detection, remediation and validation across web applications, APIs and code, and fitting into both developer and AppSec workflows. title: EU makes progress towards PHP patching, UK lags behind
raw_text:
Organisations across the European Union (EU) are leading the charge to address the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, with patch rates hitting about 50% of exposed hosts in the Netherlands, the DACH – Austria, Germany and Switzerland – countries edging closer to 40%, and Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia and Finland hovering at around 30%.

However, British organisations are lagging behind, with barely a quarter of exposed hosts identified as located in the UK patched, while in the US things are moving even slower, with just under 20% of hosts now secured.

Globally, as of 12pm on Monday 26 October, 412,000 publicly accessible PHP hosts were patched, representing about 19% of the visible total.

This is according to live data provided by UK-based cyber startup Infrawatch, which has been tracking PHP2Shell patching rates since last week.

Meanwhile, evidence is stacking up that successful real-world compromises of PHP2Shell are now a reality. According to Bleeping Computer, a Perplexity researcher confirmed they observed remote code execution (RCE) exploiting PHP2Shell after setting up honeypots running a vulnerable version of PHP.

“The news that the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are now being successfully exploited in the wild isn’t surprising, but it adds even great urgency towards patching,” said Keith Simpson, group operations head at Converged Solutions Group, an Aberdeen-based managed services provider (MSP)

“When major vulnerabilities are disclosed, threat actors move quickly to find ways to exploit them, and AI is now accelerating these efforts. The gap between disclosure and exploitation is shrinking and is often even shorter than the time organisations require to apply patches.

Simpson warned: “While websites have been taken down across the globe, this is not a long-term solution. Many organisations will still not have patched, and they cannot overlook the threat. They must act today.”

This said, confirmation of successful PHP2Shell exploitation – even in a non-impactful honeypot environment – strongly suggests that threat actors have likely already compromised vulnerable real-world systems.

Over the coming days and weeks, this likely means that the opportunistic scanning activity seen to date will begin to morph into web shell deployment and credential theft, followed by brokered access sales to other cyber criminals, and ultimately, a spate of ransomware activity.

Business analysis firm Moodys said that observed exploitation seemed to be originating from multiple threat actors, and exposure is likely to remain uneven, with SMEs with more limited cyber postures facing greater challenges in identifying and fixing vulnerable instances.

This, said Moodys, could increase the likelihood of a ‘long tail’ of individual cyber compromises affecting organisations for months to come.

And according to threat intel company Cyfirma, there is also now evidence that PHP2Shell is attracting the interest of nation-state affiliated threat actors. The firm’s researchers said they were confident that a North Korean-nexus threat actor associated with the infamous Lazarus Group is “actively staging a global offensive campaign” against vulnerable, internet-facing PHP runtimes.

In addition to merely applying the patches, this means security teams should also be activating threat detection and response procedures to ascertain whether or not a breach is in progress.

title: UK secrecy over AI in immigration and asylum decisions under fire
raw_text:
The government is using AI in “near total secrecy” to police immigration and border crossings and is routinely invoking “national security” to refuse to answer questions on its use of automated technology, it is claimed.

MPs and campaigners warned today that secrecy around the Home Office’s use of AI in asylum and immigration meant there was little accountability over the UK’s use of the technology or its effectiveness.

Migrants and people crossing into the UK were at risk of discrimination, biased decision making and of being wrongly identified by facial-recognition systems, according to research by the Open Rights Group (ORG).

The campaign group warns in a 100-page report that the government is using “technical fixes” – what it calls “tech no-solutionism” – to implement policy decisions around “the complex human phenomenon of migration”.

The Home Office has embedded AI into systems used to monitor borders through live facial recognition and is using AI-powered drones and surveillance towers to monitor small boat crossings.

It is also using AI to estimate the ages of people seeking asylum, to summarise case interviews of asylum seekers, to analyse the contents of mobile phones, to automatically identify sham marriages, and to prioritise immigration cases.

UK locked-in to overseas technology

Most of the technology used is supplied by US, Israeli and other foreign defence and security companies, leaving the UK potentially locked-in to overseas technology, rather than developing its own AI solutions.

The report warns AI can make mistakes, produce inaccurate information, leave out important details or present wrong information in a way that makes it appear reliable, with “ruinous” consequences for asylum seekers.

Computer Weekly previously reported that the Home Office’s Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) tool, which is used to summarise interviews with asylum seekers, had been deployed despite a significant proportion of summaries failing quality and accuracy checks.

Another algorithmic tool, Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (IPIC), automatically recommends migrants for actions, including detention and bail conditions.

According to research by the campaign group Privacy International, the algorithm is designed to push case workers into accepting its recommendations by requiring officials to provide an explanation if they disagree.

IPIC uses nationality to inform its decisions, leading to risks that people with certain nationalities could be more likely to receive negative decisions, such as being recommended for detention or electronic tagging, the report claims.

Another system, the Electronic Monitoring Review Tool (EMRT), automatically generates “harm scores” to determine how long people should wear ankle tags before being moved to other forms of monitoring.

Atlas

The Home Office uses the Atlas platform to manage the casework for immigration and asylum applications, using automated tools to select and deliver data to caseworkers for decision making.

Leaked documents reported by the Guardian revealed that flaws with the database led to more than 76,000 people being listed with incorrect names, photographs or immigration status.

Published contracts reveal that Atlas is due to be enhanced with AI, as part of an £87m deal with Mastek, an IT service provider with headquarters in India, though no details have been disclosed.

Under another Home Office contract, Mastek is providing AI to enhance the government’s Biometric Services Gateway and National DNA database for immigration and asylum purposes.

Age estimation

The Home Office is trialling AI to estimate the ages of people seeking asylum, after awarding a contract for facial age estimation (FAE) in May to UK-based Akhter Computers and Germany’s Cognitec Systems.

The trials, expected to be carried out at the Western Jet Foil processing centre in Dover, will focus on 16-18 year olds, but even the best technology has an error margin of 2.5 years, creating risks that juveniles will be wrongly identified as adults.

Human rights groups warn that the technology has more difficulty estimating the ages of women and people of colour, and that children seeking asylum often appear prematurely aged due to trauma, violence, lack of food and sleep and exposure to salt water during dangerous sea crossings.

Mobile phone data extraction

In January, new powers in the Border Security Asylum and Immigration Act 2025, came into force allowing immigration officers to extract data from asylum seeker’s mobile phones, with trials beginning in Manston migrant processing centre in Kent.

Extracting phone data is likely to use tools from suppliers such as the Israeli company Cellebrite, which uses AI to analyse call records, text messages, images and videos stored on mobile phones and other electronic devices at high speed.

The Home Office is using a machine learning tool to automate the detection of sham marriages, based on six undisclosed risk factors, which according to the report has disproportionately selected a limited range of nationalities – despite any evidence that they are more likely than other nationalities to be involved in sham marriages.

Border surveillance

The UK has taken part in EU-funded projects aimed to develop powerful surveillance capabilities at borders. They include CarMen, which promises the real-time biometric identification of passengers in vehicles moving up to 20 km/h; and PopEye, which aims to identify multiple travellers crossing a border on foot or in a vehicle from up to 200 meters away.

Multiple pilots of live facial recognition are being conducted at Holyhead in Anglesey, Wales, to identify people returning to the UK in breach of deportation orders.

A trial in April scanned thousands of faces of people traveling from Dublin to Holyhead but produced no matches, raising questions about the effectiveness and proportionality of the technology, according to a report by the Irish Times.

Anduril Sentry Towers

The Home Office’s use of AI-powered surveillance towers was revealed by journalist and researcher Samuel Storey. The towers, supplied by US defence firm Anduril, use an AI-based operating system to produce a real-time picture of the border and to identify and track individuals of interest.

The Home Office put Storey under pressure to remove details of the locations of the towers he had identified, claiming both that they were inaccurate and likely to lead to countermeasures by criminals.

Investigations have also revealed that the Home Office uses drones produced by foreign security companies, including Tekever in Portugal and Israel’s Elbit Systems, to patrol the channel to identify small boats. Computer Weekly previously reported Home Office plans to deploy AI-powered satellites to counter small boat crossings.

Call to address gaps in regulation

The Open Rights Group calls for the government to address gaps in regulation of AI systems, including banning the use of mass live surveillance in public places and regulating high-risk applications of AI. There should be transparency about government use of AI, including a robust public register of AI tools, and a rejection of “AI techno-solutionism”, it said.

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that the Home Office had been reluctant to publish documents to explain how AI is used in asylum processing. “The Home Office has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks,” she added.

SNP MP Pete Wishart criticised the Home Office’s failure to inform asylum applicants when AI is used in their cases, meaning they could not challenge their decisions. “There is also an important question of accountability. If an asylum seeker believes that an AI system has made a mistake, they need to be able to know that the technology was used and have the chance to challenge its output,” he added.

Green Party MP Sian Berry said that testing AI on migrants has consequences for the rest of society, including normalising biometric checks, digital identification and sharing data on individuals.

“Artificial intelligence systems must be subject to clear laws founded in human rights and fairness, with decisions subject to scrutiny and challenge. Human beings need to make decisions about people, and not rely on opaque calculations,” she added.

She said that public bodies should not hand over democratic control of the way technology is designed and deployed to “a handful of corporations with dubious human rights records”.

Claudia Aradau, professor of international politics at King’s College London, said that AI systems amplified biases in the data used to train them, and created a hostile environment for immigrants. “These systems do not just amplify existing social biases in the data but produce hostility as both an intended and unintended consequence,” she said.

AI tools do not replace humans

A Home Office spokesperson said that artificial intelligence is just one of the tools available and does not replace or automate the role of human decision makers.

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” the spokesperson added.

“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

title: Employees must be empowered to refuse AI tools at work, says UTAW
raw_text:
Employees should be empowered to refuse the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools at work, says the tech worker union, after finding employers are using the technology to intensify workloads, eliminate junior hiring and rationalise redundancies.

Conducted by the United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) union – a branch of the Communication Workers Union (CWU) – the AI workers’ inquiry 2026 explores how AI tools are reshaping labour practices from the perspective of workers throughout the tech sector.

Focused less on the technology’s functionality and more on who controls and benefits from it, the inquiry found that AI technology was “a largely negative force” in the workplace, leading to a widespread deskilling and degrading of expertise, expanded surveillance, less accountability for managers and weaker job security.

The worker-led inquiry also found that AI, despite being touted as a productivity-boosting technology that can reduce working time, is being used in practice to increase and intensify people’s workloads.

All of this is taking place, it added, without workers having a meaningful say over how AI technologies are introduced.

“Workers stressed that positive uses depend on their ability to decide for themselves how to engage with AI,” said a report on the inquiry’s findings. “The central problem is not simply whether AI works well, but how it is introduced, controlled, measured and used by employers. Put simply, it is useful only when one gets to choose if and how to use them.”

It added that workers must be actively empowered to defend and extend their rights over how AI is used, which should include being given “enforceable power” over how it is deployed in the workplace, as an antidote to its unilateral imposition from management.

‘Testing ground’

UTAW highlighted how, according to inquiry participants, senior management teams do not understand the tools they are mandating, and are using staff as a “testing ground” for tools that often either slow down or worsen the work they claim to speed up or improve.

The unilateral imposition of AI, UTAW added, is also part of a wider trend where AI is being used to reduce headcounts and avoid hiring, while distributing the remaining work to fewer employees under tighter deadlines.

“At first glance, companies are carrying out redundancies (both mass layoffs and small regular redundancy exercises) and claiming this is because ‘AI is replacing the need for workers’,” it said.

“Workers on the inside report that layoffs are more often to maintain revenue in the face of rising inflation, to increase company valuation by manipulating financial indices, or even to cover the cost of GenAI [generative AI] platform subscriptions.

“These so-called AI efficiencies are an excuse to obfuscate a reality where skilled staff are replaced with new tools that do not work well while workers who survive redundancy pick up the ever-intensifying slack.”

For those at the start of their careers, UTAW also highlighted how AI is undermining their ability to develop skills, because they are either becoming too reliant on the tech themselves, or their employer is outsourcing their work – which would help them develop foundational skills – to automation.

“Junior workers and those without strong foundational skills are becoming overly reliant on tools such as agents and assistants,” it said. “There is no incentive or time for juniors to learn the necessary technical and critical thinking skills; work intensification means they are increasingly being denied a sounding board to chat through problems.

“Employers are using LLMs [large language models] as a substitute for training their employees, obscuring gaps in subject-matter expertise and skills … The long-term trajectory is a loss of expertise and skills across the sector.”

Policy proposals

As a result of its findings, UTAW has made a number of policy proposals for AI at work.

These include protecting employees from disciplinary and performance processes which are based on how much they are using (or not using) AI tools; strengthening redundancy protections so employers cannot use AI adoption as cover for offshoring or outsourcing; and introducing a statutory duty on employers to “meaningfully consult” workers before AI tools are deployed.

It added that, where collective bargaining agreements exist, employers must have a duty to negotiate on AI deployments and their associated effects.

Where these agreements do not exist, UTAW said that workers must still be given a right to refuse AI “where there are professional, ethical, environmental, equality, accessibility, safety, religious, mental health or quality concerns” around its use.

The codification of a right to refuse should also be accompanied by protections for workers that refuse, question or otherwise criticise an employer’s use of AI.

A number of other proposals also called for increased transparency around AI deployments at work.

This includes more consistent disclosures on its environmental impacts, such as “energy use, water use, datacentre dependency, infrastructure demand and supply-chain impacts”; the publication of various pre-deployment impact assessments; and prohibiting the use of opaque, AI-driven work evaluations.

To ensure employers are held accountable, UTAW concluded there is a need to establish a new regulatory authority on AI at work, which has statutory powers to investigate, enforce and sanction both employers and their technology providers.

“The authority should have the power to require employers to disclose AI systems, pause deployment, carry out impact assessments, consult workers and their unions, remedy harm, and withdraw deployed systems,” it said, adding that any governance board “should include expert worker and trade union representation equal to the number of representatives of employers, civil servants and academics”.

This includes more consistent disclosures on its environmental impacts, such as “energy use, water use, datacentre dependency, infrastructure demand and supply-chain impacts”; the publication of various pre-deployment impact assessments; and prohibiting the use of opaque, AI-driven work evaluations.

To ensure employers are held accountable, UTAW concluded there is a need to establish a new regulatory authority on AI at work, which has statutory powers to investigate, enforce and sanction both employers and their technology providers.

“The authority should have the power to require employers to disclose AI systems, pause deployment, carry out impact assessments, consult workers and their unions, remedy harm, and withdraw deployed systems,” it said, adding that any governance board “should include expert worker and trade union representation equal to the number of representatives of employers, civil servants and academics”.

title: ‘Blackmail’ call as Warwickshire council approves £9m Microsoft renewal
raw_text:
Warwickshire County Council’s Reform-run cabinet has approved the procurement of a three-year Microsoft 365 licence renewal worth about £9m. The move was dubbed “blackmail” by its former leader as the approval went through.

The decision report – introduced by Reform councillor Michael Bannister – commits the council to a renewal agreement that runs from June 2027 to May 2030. The cost is roughly £3m a year, and that’s about £375,000, or 15%, more than the council pays currently. Bannister attributed the rise principally to Microsoft’s pricing changes across the public sector, after the previous renewal had deferred increases by continuing existing national pricing arrangements.

Warwickshire County Council – which rolled out Microsoft cloud in 2019 – buys through the government’s Microsoft aggregation route, which uses collective public sector buying power to secure pricing. Confirmation of the award is subject to a licence count review of active users, allocations and optional products. 

The report prepared for council cabinet approval describes the licences as “business critical”, in that they underpin “core productivity, collaboration, information management, security and analytics capabilities”, as well as cyber security, data protection and the groundwork for automation and artificial intelligence. Around 900 licences are to be charged to the relevant business areas, with further optional products potentially pushing the cost higher.

Green councillor Keith Kondakor, who represents Weddington, framed the decision as paying Microsoft for software the council would not own. Holding up a floppy disk he bought more than 40 years ago, he said: “When we bought Microsoft products in 1983, we owned them. You couldn’t get trapped, because once you bought your DOS, you got your DOS.”

His point was to draw a contrast with today’s subscription licensing. “The problem now is that we’re getting trapped into paying licence fees. We licence for a year or three years and then Microsoft can whack the price up,” he said.

He noted the French government is moving away from Microsoft, and warned: “If you are beholden to an American corporation, things can change.”

Rob Howard, Reform UK’s former council leader now serving as portfolio holder for economy, replied. He did not dispute the framing. “You’ve echoed what we were talking about in our pre-meeting,” he said. “I think we are all shocked about the amount of money this is going to cost us. We have no choice on this occasion, I’m afraid.”

His reasoning was that there was too little time to stand up an alternative before the May 2027 expiry. But he accepted the longer-term risk. “You’re right, we don’t want to be held with this sort of blackmail over the next 10 years. It is going to be more next time round,” he said.

The exchange came as the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) considers designating Microsoft’s business software ecosystem with strategic market status, while Microsoft contests the premise of the investigation.

The report warned that failing to approve the procurement risked “poorer commercial outcomes and disruption to essential digital services”. It also flagged that the agreement may overlap with local government reorganisation, with licence numbers, transfers and potential duplicate costs to be resolved before award.

The decision approves the procurement in principle. Any actual award rests with the executive director for resources, subject to affordability, completion of procurement and legal and financial assurance, while the extra £375,000 a year still has to be found within the budget.

title: How Luxembourg built a secure sovereign instant messaging service for residents
raw_text:
Luxembourg, one of Europe’s smallest countries with a population of just under 700,000, has big ambitions for its state-backed encrypted messaging service.

Luxchat, a secure “sovereign” instant messaging service for government, citizens and businesses, has its origins in the 2020 Covid pandemic.

Faced with working remotely, civil servants turned to unofficial messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal to carry out the business of government during the crisis.

That raised concerns about the security of government information and the unencrypted metadata that accompanied each message, which could identify who was talking to whom in government, as it passed through servers and datacentres outside the country.

Data sovereignty has a long history in Luxembourg. All communication service providers, including mobile phone operators Orange and Proximus, use a backbone network provided by Luxembourg Internet Exchange (LU-CIX), which ensures communications within Luxembourg stay within Luxembourg.

After Covid, Luxembourg’s Ministry for Digitalisation worked with LU-CIX on a project to develop a secure national alternative encrypted messaging system, hosted entirely within Luxembourg’s borders.

Sovereign alternative to WhatsApp

Claude Demuth is the chairman of LU-CIX, which maintains the Luxchat app. He told Computer Weekly that while WhatsApp and Signal were not recommended for government use, in practice there was no practical alternative for government workers in Europe during the pandemic.

“We saw that we needed a more independent sovereign communication service in Luxembourg. We wanted a solution not only for the government and for civil servants, but also for the population and businesses,” he said.

The Grand Duchy opted to use the open source end-to-end encrypted communications protocol, Matrix, with support from French-UK technology company Element, to build a secure government instant messaging network.

Demuth said choosing an open source technology meant Luxembourg could use multiple suppliers to support the network, avoiding the risks of being locked in to a single supplier.

Looking for security backdoors

Open source also offered greater security, making it possible for experts to check the Matrix code to ensure that there were no hidden security backdoors – a requirement of the Luxembourg government.

Luxembourg tested its first Matrix messenger prototypes in 2021 with government ministries and agencies before the project got the go-ahead from the government in summer 2022.

In May 2023, Luxembourg launched the first iteration of the app, Luxchat4Gov, which provides instant messaging services for civil servants.

Today, the app has 14,000 users across education, central government and local administrations, out of a potential 64,000 users.

Luxchat is available from four suppliers – including LU-CIX – which run the app on their own servers hosted in Luxembourg, providing a distributed service that gives the messaging service greater resilience should a failure occur in one part of the network.

Data is kept private

The suppliers have to agree to minimum security levels, and are prohibited from selling data, including metadata, or offering advertising to people who use the messaging app.

Matrix messenger services have been deployed across Europe, including in France, which runs TChap; in Belgium, which runs BEAM; and in Germany, which has deployed the BundesMessenger for government and its armed forces.

Luxembourg claims to be the only country to have deployed an instant messaging service for government that is interoperable with messaging services used by the public and businesses.

The app comes in three versions – Luxchat, Luxchat4Gov and a version for business, Luxchat4Pro, that offers backup communications in a crisis.

Three Luxchat options

Luxchat: Free end-to-end instant messaging service for residents and businesses in Luxembourg. Users can share text messages, documents, images and videos either with individuals or in group chatrooms. The service is operated by multiple providers that agree to respect the privacy of their users and their personal data, and to keep the service free of advertising.

Luxchat4Pro: Paid instant messaging services for companies and organisations. Offers advanced security, IT integration and customisation.

Luxhchat4Gov: Instant messaging service for civil servants.

How Luxembourg adapted Matrix

Demuth said building the back-end IT for Luxchat, including building redundancy and backup servers, while not easy, was “doable” with the help of good engineers.

A bigger challenge was that the Matrix app, based on an implementation by the French-UK company Element, did not completely meet Luxembourg’s requirements.

“We had to adapt to add even more security,” he said. That meant that Luxchat is a variant or “fork” of the Element standard. However, LU-CIX is still able to benefit from updates by Element.

“We keep our app close to the Element app, so if they maintain the app, our app will be maintained with some delay,” Demuth added.

Luxchat is available on four platforms: Android, iPhone, Windows and Apple. It is also accessible through the web.

“The back end is great – the communication, the concept, the protocol. It works fine. The challenge is always the app, and the user experience is always difficult,” he said.

“Everyone has installed apps from big players, with big money behind them and with great quality. We are coming in here, in Europe, with a new app, and the challenge is to match the quality and have new features,” Demuth added.

Directory services

Further development work went into building a directory to help people find each other, which is not a standard feature of the Element app.

For the government version of Luxchat, every government employee is included in the directory. For the public app, people have the choice to opt in or out of the directory.

App users can share their ID with others to invite them to join conversations, even if they are not listed.

Critical national infrastructure

The standard Luxchat app, which is paid for by sponsoring partners, including the Luxembourg Chamber of Commerce, can store messages for only two years before they are deleted, and has no service-level agreement.

Companies that provide critical national infrastructure in Luxembourg use the professional version of the messaging service, which is hosted on a separate server with a separate security configuration. It offers longer storage and a service level agreement.

Companies use it largely for business-to-business communications, but in time, Demuth anticipates that businesses will increasingly use Luxchat to communicate with customers. For example, an electricity provider, instead of using email, could use Luxchat to deliver the electricity bill as a secure PDF.

Luxchat main partners

  • LU-CIX
  • Luxembourg Chamber of Commerce
  • Ministry for Digitalisation

Supported by:

  • Information Technology Management Center for Education (CGIE)
  • Luxembourg House of Cybersecurity (LCH)
  • Restena Foundation, national research and education network
  • Post Luxembourg

Technical partners:

  • Agilepartner
  • BCE
  • The national geoportal of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg
  • LuxID – digital ID provider hosted in Post Luxembourg datacentres

Verifying identity

According to Patrick Webber, a civil servant at the Ministry for Digitalisation, one of the biggest challenges is verifying the identities of people using Luxchat.

The government has a public sector identity service in place to allow government employees to securely identify themselves. There are also several identity providers in the private sector used by companies to verify their employees.

“The vision of the public and private sector is that every man and woman living in Luxembourg will have Luxchat and a verified log-in,” Demuth told Computer Weekly.

Future plans

Luxembourg residents will be able to use Luxchat to conduct business with the government, acting as a more secure replacement for email.

For example, they might use the messaging service to buy a parking permit, or parents might use it to speak to their children’s teachers. It could be used to hire a bicycle, rent a car, or receive a code to pick up a parcel from a delivery company.

There are also plans to integrate Luxchat into the health service in Luxembourg, allowing patients to meet online with their doctors, or to securely exchange medical information.

“We are in discussions with the healthcare sector, and the vision is that in one to three years, the healthcare industry and the population will be using Luxchat,” he said. “The healthcare sector again wants a national, sovereign, independent and secure solution.”

One of the challenges will be to persuade younger people to use the app, but the hope is that Luxchat will become more popular as more people use it to access government and business services.

“The people who are using Luxchat are mostly between 20 and 60 years of age. They are aware of security and sovereignty,” said Demuth.

In contrast, younger people tend to use platforms such as Discord, Snapchat and Instagram, and are less concerned about the security of their data.

title: Lost in the post: Subpostmasters could miss out on redress
raw_text:
Former subpostmasters and family members could miss out on financial redress owed to them by the Post Office due to the passage of time.

The Post Office Horizon scandal has already seen nearly £2bn paid in compensation for losses and suffering to subpostmasters past and present, but despite the scandal’s high public profile since ITV’s dramatisation of it, some elderly former subpostmasters were not aware of what they were owed in time to apply.

Many had problems decades ago, some have suffered illness and others have died in the years since, but new cases are emerging, and some deserving of redress could miss out unless changes to rules are made.

Former subpostmasters were entitled to a £75,000 fixed sum award under the Horizon Shortfall Scheme (HSS) if they had evidence of any unexplained shortfalls. This particular redress scheme has paid out over £1bn to subpostmasters.

The statutory public inquiry into the scandal agreed to a date of midnight 27 November 2025, when no claims for financial redress under HSS could be made after. The Post Office accepted this recommendation, but decided on a later date of 31 January 2026.

However, Computer Weekly has spoken to elderly former subpostmasters that were not even aware of the redress scheme until it was too late to apply and had applications rejected. Others have only discovered letters from the Post Office when their former subpostmaster parents have died.

Last week, the government reconfirmed its commitment to providing compensation to every effected subpostmaster and “strengthening fairness”, but there is a cohort fighting for acceptance on redress schemes.

Raft of changes

In a recent statement after announcing a raft of changes to redress schemes, Post Office minister Kate Dearden said: “We remain unwavering in our commitment to provide fair, comprehensive and timely redress to all those affected and ensure that a scandal like this never happens again.”

Chris Head, a former subpostmaster and victim of the scandal turned campaigner, said: “The Post Office says it wants to make sure that everybody who’s eligible receives their redress, but at the same time, there are people that are, for all sorts of different reasons, not going to receive it because they are refused access to a scheme.”

Head said he is currently supporting about half a dozen cases where this is an issue.

One case is that of Robert Nichol, a former subpostmaster who ran a Post Office branch in the village of Dalston, Cumbria, from 1982 to 2004.

Speaking on his behalf, his wife, Anne Nichol, said they had problems with Horizon, with regular unexplainable shortfalls after being forced to replace paper-based accounting methods with the software in 2000. By 2004, Nichol resigned as a subpostmaster because “he just couldn’t cope with Horizon anymore”, said his wife.

Now, the couple face being left out of financial redress schemes. Anne Nichol said the couple, who have moved several times since giving up their branch, never received any correspondence from the Post Office regarding the redress they could apply for, and when they finally applied to the Horizon Shortfalls Scheme in March, they were rejected due its closure. The Post Office claims it sent letters to Mr Nichol.

The first letter sent by the Nichols claiming redress was on 30 March, just two months after HSS closed for new applications at the end of January this year. “We’ve got eight emails of rejection, all saying the same thing,” Mrs Nichol told Computer Weekly.

The latest Post Office rejection letter said: “We have reviewed the points you have raised and the information provided. We acknowledge your comments regarding not receiving correspondence about the HSS, your personal circumstances, and your views on the handling of late applications. However, as previously advised, the HSS is now closed to new applications. It is not possible to accept new applications under the scheme, and there is no appeals process in relation to this decision.”

It continued: “We note your reference to comments made regarding exceptional criteria and your ongoing discussions with your MP, together with your request for personal data. However, these matters do not alter the position regarding your application to the HSS. Accordingly, our position remains unchanged. We are unable to accept your application and we now consider this matter closed.”

Computer Weekly contacted the Nichols’ MP, Markus Campbell-Savours, who has been informed of their predicament, but he had not responded when this article was published.

Hope for some

The Post Office has shown some flexibility and, according to Head, one former subpostmaster who applied to the Post Office Process Review (PPR) scheme, which was set up to provide redress for losses related to non-Horizon processes, was put into the HSS after the Post Office spotted something in the claim which it believed justified it. This was despite the HSS being closed.

Writing on a Facebook page set up by people affected by the scandal, the former subpostmaster, who ran a branch from 2014 to 2023, wrote: “I completed a PPR claim form as a mains branch that experienced many problems … I received a phone call inviting me to apply for the fixed rate [£75,000] or full enquiry. I was told only, ‘Something on your application led us to extend the deadline’ – no detail given.”

Head said: “Within that claim for PPR, Post Office has seen something either in their evidence or in their own data that suggests the applicant should receive a payment under the other scheme. Therefore, they’re inviting them to make a late claim even though it’s closed. And that flies in the face of how the Nichols have been treated.”

Sir Alan Bates, who led the subpostmasters’ fight for justice, agreed there will inevitably be many subpostmasters that qualify for compensation but have not applied, whether because they didn’t know about it or they don’t want to be involved with the Post Office.

“I actually met somebody last week whose father had been prosecuted and had losses related to Capture software, and they felt it was all too late to apply,” he told Computer Weekly.

Bates hopes, when the Post Office scandal public inquiry reports, “it brings it back into the public conscious as such, and maybe that will help revive it”.

Furthermore, Head described a case where a former subpostmaster had passed away, after suffering from severe dementia, and his family found the forms for applying for redress in the house, which because of his illness, he hadn’t acted upon.

A Post Office spokesperson said: “The Horizon Shortfall Scheme was open for applications between 2020 and 2026 and to date, over £1 billion has been paid to over 13,000 people through the scheme. Inquiry chair Sir Wyn Williams recommended that the scheme should close and Post Office accepted that recommendation. The Horizon Shortfall Scheme closed to new applications on 31 January 2026.

“Ahead of the closure date, we used a national media advertising campaign, targeted social media adverts, and sent invitation and reminder letters to make people aware of the closure date and their eligibility for the scheme. For the invitation and reminder letters, we used address tracing and specialist next of kin tracing to ensure we could reach as many people as possible. Applications submitted for a period after the 31 January 2026 deadline would have been considered in special circumstances.”

summary:
Former subpostmasters and family members could miss out on financial redress owed to them by the Post Office due to the passage of time.

The Post Office Horizon scandal has already seen nearly £2bn paid in compensation for losses and suffering to subpostmasters past and present, but despite the scandal’s high public profile since ITV’s dramatisation of it, some elderly former subpostmasters were not aware of what they were owed in time to apply.

Many had problems decades ago, some have suffered illness and others have died in the years since, but new cases are emerging, and some deserving of redress could miss out unless changes to rules are made.

Former subpostmasters were entitled to a £75,000 fixed sum award under the Horizon Shortfall Scheme (HSS) if they had evidence of any unexplained shortfalls. This particular redress scheme has paid out over £1bn to subpostmasters.

The statutory public inquiry into the scandal agreed to a date of midnight 27 November 2025, when no claims for financial redress under HSS could be made after. The Post Office accepted this recommendation, but decided on a later date of 31 January 2026.

However, Computer Weekly has spoken to elderly former subpostmasters that were not even aware of the redress scheme until it was too late to apply and had applications rejected. Others have only discovered letters from the Post Office when their former subpostmaster parents have died.

Last week, the government reconfirmed its commitment to providing compensation to every effected subpostmaster and “strengthening fairness”, but there is a cohort fighting for acceptance on redress schemes.

Raft of changes

In a recent statement after announcing a raft of changes to redress schemes, Post Office minister Kate Dearden said: “We remain unwavering in our commitment to provide fair, comprehensive and timely redress to all those affected and ensure that a scandal like this never happens again.”

Chris Head, a former subpostmaster and victim of the scandal turned campaigner, said: “The Post Office says it wants to make sure that everybody who’s eligible receives their redress, but at the same time, there are people that are, for all sorts of different reasons, not going to receive it because they are refused access to a scheme.”

Head said he is currently supporting about half a dozen cases where this is an issue.

One case is that of Robert Nichol, a former subpostmaster who ran a Post Office branch in the village of Dalston, Cumbria, from 1982 to 2004.

Speaking on his behalf, his wife, Anne Nichol, said they had problems with Horizon, with regular unexplainable shortfalls after being forced to replace paper-based accounting methods with the software in 2000.

title: Financial services leaders believe AI impact will be bigger than Big Bang
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) technology will have a greater impact on the finance sector than the sweeping changes made in 1986, known as the Big Bang.

According to KPMG’s UK Financial Services Sentiment Survey, 87% of UK financial sector leaders believe this to be the case.

Deregulation and reforms to the finance sector in 1986 included the introduction of electronic trading. The events boosted London to the extent that it arguably became the most important finance centre in the world. Paper-based practices disappeared and finance firms and trading rooms became unrecognisable.

According to KPMG, about nine out of 10 finance leaders think technology changes driven by AI will have an even greater impact on the industry.

Commenting on the findings, Fiona Fry, an independent non-executive director and former KPMG partner, who began her financial services career during the Big Bang, said that when she started working in the City, technology was minimal.

“Memos were handwritten and delivered, communications between organisations were by letter, and most computer programs were very basic, requiring mostly manual inputs. The days of being ‘always on’ had not arrived, as technology did not follow you home,” she said.

Fry added that there have been many changes over the following decades, but AI will “dwarf” them all.

“From the advent of the BlackBerry, to being connected globally, to instant information and analysis on our smartphones and via the cloud, the financial sector has seen a transformation in how it uses data, leading to a constant evolution of business models,” she said.

“[But] AI will dwarf the technological developments I have seen over four decades. It will enable firms to understand their competitive performance in a way not previously imagined, providing far more in-depth analysis of product performance and customer behaviour, thus enabling those who embrace it to thrive and grow. Customers will benefit too, being provided with financial products more targeted towards their specific needs.”

AI will spread finance

Another key difference between the Big Bang’s impact and that of AI, according to the KPMG survey, is that it will not just strengthen the London-centric sector, but spread the benefits.

The survey also found that 88% of financial services leaders believe AI’s benefits will be felt more widely across the UK. Just over half of respondents believe the balance between London’s financial districts and the rest of the UK should shift towards regional financial centres over the next decade. Just 21% think it should become more concentrated in the capital.

“The [finance] Big Bang generated significant growth and transformed the UK’s financial markets, but its benefits were not felt equally across the country. AI offers a different path, with financial services leaders seeing it as the next Big Bang to drive innovation and stronger long-term growth more widely across regional centres,” said Karim Haji, global and UK head of financial services at KPMG.

While the regional impact of AI will differ from that of the Big Bang, there will be a similar change to human roles across the finance sector, as the technology increasingly reduces human workloads. Fry said: “In the 1990s, some feared technology would diminish human skills; today, many worry about AI’s impact on jobs.”

These fears have been stoked by recent announcements by major UK banks Barclays and HSBC, which have seen thousands of jobs cut and replaced by AI technology.

But Fry said people adapted to the changes brought by the Big Bang in 1986, and the same will be the case with AI. “In my view, just as computers brought an end to the office postie, AI will mean fewer highly repetitive jobs, while human judgement in assurance, risk identification and oversight will become more important, not less.”
